'''Scott Duncan Tremaine''' (born 1950)<ref name = "ACBIO">{{cite web|url = http://www.astro-canada.ca/_en/a2219.html|title = Scott Duncan Tremaine (1950– )
|publisher = Virtual Museum of Canada|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.utpress.utoronto.ca/cgi-bin/cw2w3.cgi?p=tougas&t=48217&d=1404|title = Scott Duncan TREMAINE|work = Canadian Who's Who 1997 edition on the web|publisher = University of Toronto Press}}{{dead link|date=September 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> is a Canadian-born [[Astrophysics|astrophysicist]]. He is a fellow of the [[Royal Society of London]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/Lists-of-Royal-Society-Fellows-1660-2007/ |title=Lists of Royal Society Fellows 1660–2007 |publisher=The Royal Society |accessdate=18 July 2010 |location=London |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100324095152/http://royalsociety.org/Lists-of-Royal-Society-Fellows-1660-2007/ |archivedate=24 March 2010 }}</ref> the [[Royal Society of Canada]] and the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.towntopics.com/aug2306/other5.html|title = Tremaine Follows Bahcall's Stellar Path at the Institute|work = [[Town Topics (newspaper)|Town Topics]]|accessdate = 9 April 2007|archive-date = 3 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303165554/http://www.towntopics.com/aug2306/other5.html|url-status = dead}}</ref> Tremaine is widely regarded as one of the world's leading astrophysicists<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/the-institute-letter/|title = The Institute Letter|publisher= Institute for Advanced Studies|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070403214554/http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/the-institute-letter/ <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 3 April 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin2/020129b.asp|title = Bond awarded Dannie Heineman Prize|publisher = University of Toronto|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070404214854/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin2/020129b.asp <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 4 April 2007}}</ref> for his contributions to the theory of [[Solar System]] and [[galaxy|galactic]] [[Relativistic dynamics|dynamics]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.srac.ca/education/asteroids.shtml|title = Canadian Asteroids|publisher = Royal Astronomical Society of Canada|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070106173741/http://www.srac.ca/education/asteroids.shtml|archivedate = 6 January 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref> Tremaine is the [[namesake]] of asteroid [[3806 Tremaine]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://exn.ca/Stories/1997/03/04/03.asp|title = Asteroid 3806 named after eminent Canadian astrophysicist|publisher = Discovery Channel|accessdate = 9 April 2007|archive-date = 29 September 2007|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070929091511/http://exn.ca/Stories/1997/03/04/03.asp|url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/march17_97/art1.htm|title = Look, up in the Sky|publisher = University of Toronto|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070404205809/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/march17_97/art1.htm <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 4 April 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mcmaster.ca/ua/opr/times/spring97/alumalb.htm |title=McMaster Times – Spring 1997 |accessdate=28 May 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20050929052433/http://www.mcmaster.ca/ua/opr/times/spring97/alumalb.htm |archivedate=29 September 2005 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.astro.utoronto.ca/asteroids.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20021117064932/http://www.astro.utoronto.ca/asteroids.html|url-status = dead|archive-date = 17 November 2002|title = Asteroids (minor planets) related to UofT people|accessdate = 28 May 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref> He is credited with coining the name "[[Kuiper belt]]".<ref>{{cite book|title=Beyond Pluto: Exploring the outer limits of the solar system |author=John Davies|publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=2001|pages=191}}</ref>

==Career==
He obtained a bachelor's degree at [[McMaster University]] in 1971, and a PhD from [[Princeton University]] in 1975.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ias.edu/about/faculty-and-emeriti/tremaine|publisher = Institute for Advanced Study|title = Institute for Advanced Study: Faculty and Emeriti: Tremaine|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070129040407/http://www.ias.edu/about/faculty-and-emeriti/tremaine|archivedate = 29 January 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref> He further received an honorary PhD from McMaster University in 1996.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june3_96/awards.htm|title = Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics|publisher = University of Toronto's The Bulletin|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070404210655/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june3_96/awards.htm <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 4 April 2007}}</ref> He was an associate professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] from 1981 to 1985.<ref name=CUPCMCGILL>{{cite web|url = http://www.ugrad.physics.mcgill.ca/~cupc/english/speakers.html#tremaine|publisher = Canadian Undergraduate Physics Conference|title = Featured speakers for the CUPC 2003|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20041207085646/http://www.ugrad.physics.mcgill.ca/~cupc/english/speakers.html#tremaine|archivedate = 7 December 2004|df = dmy-all}}</ref> He became the first director of the [[Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics]] at the [[University of Toronto]] in 1986, a position he held until the end of his ten-year term in 1996.<ref name=CUPCMCGILL /> He gained the rare distinction of "University Professor" at the University of Toronto in 1995.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june9_97/awards.htm|title = Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics|publisher = University of Toronto Bulletin|accessdate = 30 May 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070524001851/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june9_97/awards.htm <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 24 May 2007}}</ref> In 1997, he left CITA and took up a position as a professor at Princeton University, becoming chair of the Astrophysical Sciences department from 1998 to 2006.<ref name = "ACBIO" />

Scott Tremaine is currently a professor at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], for which he left Princeton University in 2007, being replaced as department chair by [[David Spergel]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.ias.edu/newsroom/announcements/view/tremaine.html|publisher = Institute for Advanced Study|title = ASTROPHYSICIST SCOTT TREMAINE JOINS THE FACULTY OF THE INSTITUTE FOR ADVANCED STUDY|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20071219190302/http://www.ias.edu/newsroom/announcements/view/tremaine.html|archivedate = 19 December 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.physics.utoronto.ca/news_repository/top-physicist-gains-stellar-appointment/|publisher = University of Toronto|title = Top physicist gains stellar appointment|accessdate = 9 April 2007}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref> He has been married to Prof. [[Marilyn Mantei Tremaine]] for more than two decades, an expert in [[human-computer interaction]] who is the past chair of the [[SIGCHI]] section of the [[Association for Computing Machinery]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.sigchi.org/cuu/organizers.html|title = SIGCHI organizers|accessdate = 30 May 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070219165649/http://www.sigchi.org/cuu/organizers.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 19 February 2007}}</ref>

==Scientific accomplishments==
[[Image:Prometheus und Pandora.jpg|right|thumb|Pandora and Prometheus shepherding Saturn's F ring, as predicted by Goldreich and Tremaine]]
Tremaine, along with [[Peter Goldreich]], correctly predicted that [[shepherd moon]]s created [[Saturn]]'s thin [[Rings of Saturn#F Ring|F ring]], as well as the thin rings of [[Uranus]] in 1979.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.solarviews.com/eng/saturnbg.htm|title = Historical Background of Saturn's Rings|publisher = Calvin J. Hamilton|author = NASA/JPL/Ron Baalke|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.cfm?release=2002-190|title = Chaos Seen in Movement of Ring-Herding Moons of Saturn|publisher = NASA/JPL|accessdate = 9 April 2007|archive-date = 15 January 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160115062149/http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?release=2002-190|url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://partners.nytimes.com/library/national/science/062789sci-nasa-saturn.html|title = New Clues Emerge in Mystery of Planetary Rings|work = The New York Times|accessdate = 9 April 2007|date=27 June 1989}}</ref> The Saturnian moons [[Prometheus (moon)|Prometheus]] and [[Pandora (moon)|Pandora]] were first observed in 1981<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/saturn/faq.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/19991105133931/http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/saturn/faq.html|url-status = dead|archive-date = 5 November 1999|title = Frequently Asked Questions About Saturn's Rings|publisher = NASA|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref> and shepherding moons were found around Uranus' rings in 1986.<ref name="TWOHONOURS">{{cite web|url=http://www.ciar.ca/web/home.nsf/pages/home.0380 |title=Cosmologist Scott Tremaine receives two honors |publisher=Canadian Institute for Advanced Research |accessdate=9 April 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071011062904/http://www.ciar.ca/web/home.nsf/pages/home.0380 |archivedate=11 October 2007 }}</ref> Tremaine cowrote the book ''Galactic Dynamics'' with [[James Binney]], which is often regarded as the standard reference in the field<ref name = "ACBIO"/><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.astro.utoronto.ca/asteroids.html#tremaine|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20021117064932/http://www.astro.utoronto.ca/asteroids.html#tremaine|url-status = dead|archive-date = 17 November 2002|title = UofT Asteroids|publisher = University of Toronto|accessdate = 9 April 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://press.princeton.edu/titles/2537.html|author = Binney, J.|author2 = Tremaine, S.|name-list-style = amp|title = Galactic Dynamics|publisher = Princeton University Press|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070420125120/http://press.princeton.edu/titles/2537.html|archivedate = 20 April 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.cirs-tm.org/researchers/researchers.php?id=181|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927002717/http://www.cirs-tm.org/researchers/researchers.php?id=181|url-status = usurped|archive-date = 27 September 2007|title = Scott Tremaine|publisher = International Center for Scientific Research|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref><ref name = HUBROUWER>{{cite web|url = http://dda.harvard.edu/brouwer_award/brouw97.html|title = Tremaine to Receive 1997 Brouwer Award|publisher = Harvard University|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070509201421/http://dda.harvard.edu/brouwer_award/brouw97.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 9 May 2007}}</ref> and has been [[Scientific citation|cited]] more than three thousand times in scholarly publications.<ref>{{cite book|title = Citations for 1987gady.book.....B from the ADS Databases|publisher = NASA's Astrophysical Data System|bibcode = 1987gady.book.....B|year = 1987}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&lr=&client=firefox-a&cites=8438230377879290698|title = Binney:Galactic Dynamics – Google Scholar|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref> Tremaine, along with collaborators at the University of Toronto, showed that short period [[comet]]s originate in the [[Kuiper belt]].<ref>{{cite web|url = http://discovermagazine.com/1995/nov/wherecometscomef583|title = Where Comets Come From|work = Discovery Magazine|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.nytimes.com/glogin?URI=http://gk.nytimes.com/mem/gatekeeper.html&OQ=_rQ3D1Q26URIQ3DhttpQ3AQ2FQ2Fwww.nytimes.comQ2F2006Q2F09Q2F12Q2FscienceQ2FspaceQ2F12belt.htmlQ26OQ51Q3D_rQ513D1Q5126thQ5126emcQ513DthQ26OPQ3D4aaef992Q512FW@XUW)Zb5Q513AZZrHWHwwiWwQ512BWQ5124HW5bQ517EXabXW5vTbXWQ5124HUX!rQ5125KrQ515B!&OP=4be62f24Q2F9lKX9D0tKQ2BQ5Eg9StVQ2BQ3BQ3BDk9Q3ByQ3CtKStKQ5E9dQ2BtKQ20KKQ3BKyQ27StV|title = Pluto's Exotic Playmates|author = KENNETH CHANG|date = 12 September 2006|work = The New York Times|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref> Tremaine is credited with suggesting that the apparent "double nucleus" of the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] was in fact a single ring of old red stars.<ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2005/09/050921075452.htm|title = Hubble Finds Mysterious Disk of Blue Stars Around A Black Hole|work = Science Daily|accessdate = 9 April 2007}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
In 2020, he was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]].<ref> {{cite web|url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows|title=AAS Fellows|publisher=AAS|accessdate=30 September 2020}} </ref>

In 2013, he won the [[Tomalla Foundation Prize]] for his work on gravitational dynamics.

In 2010, he received an honorary doctorate from the University of Toronto "in recognition of his scholarly contributions to the field of astrophysics, and his administrative leadership in support of Canadian and international science".<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.news.utoronto.ca/media-releases/event-advisories/astrophysicist-scott-tremaine-to-receive-honoraryreceive-honorary-degree.html |title = News &#124; University of Toronto}}</ref>

In 2005, he won the Research Award from the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]].

In 2002, he was elected to membership in the [[National Academy of Sciences]].

In 1999, Tremaine also received an honorary Doctor of Science degree from St. Mary's University.

In 1998, he won the [[Brouwer Award (Division on Dynamical Astronomy)|Dirk Brouwer Award]] which is awarded by the Division of Dynamical Astronomy of the American Astronomical Society<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june9_97/awards.htm|publisher = University of Toronto|title = U. of T. The Bulletin, June 9/97, Faculty of Arts & Science|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070404205439/http://www.news.utoronto.ca/bin/bulletin/june9_97/awards.htm <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 4 April 2007}}</ref> "in recognition of his many outstanding contributions to a wide range of dynamical problems in both solar-system and galactic dynamics."<ref name = HUBROUWER />

In 1997, he was awarded the [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Astrophysics]] for "diverse and insightful applications of dynamics to planets, rings, comets, galaxies and the universe."<ref name = "TWOHONOURS" />

In 1996, he was awarded an honorary Doctor of Science award by McMaster University.

In 1994, Tremaine became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] of London and also of the [[Royal Society of Canada]].

In 1990, he was awarded the [[Rutherford Memorial Medal]] in Physics by the Academies of Arts, Humanities and Sciences of Canada for "his outstanding contributions to the field to {{sic}} astrophysics, particularly his spectacular success in predicting the properties of planetary ring dynamics and the extraplanetary objects that control them".<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.rsc.ca/index.php?page=citations_rutherford&page_id=155&lang_id=1#TOC|publisher = The Royal Society of Canada|title = RSC: The Academies of Arts, Humanities and Sciences of Canada : Rutherford Memorial Medals in Physics|accessdate = 9 April 2007 |archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927195202/http://www.rsc.ca/index.php?page=citations_rutherford&page_id=155&lang_id=1#TOC <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archivedate = 27 September 2007}}</ref>

In 1990, he won the [[C.S. Beals Award]] from the [[Canadian Astronomical Society]] which is awarded for outstanding research to a Canadian astronomer or an astronomer working in Canada.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.cascaeducation.ca/files/cdn_astronomerbeals.html#tremaine|publisher = Canadian Astronomical Society|title = Winners of the Canadian C.S. Beals Award|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070709085539/http://www.cascaeducation.ca/files/cdn_astronomerbeals.html#tremaine|archivedate = 9 July 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.astro-canada.ca/_en/a2204.html|title = Carlyle Smith Beals (1899–1979)|accessdate = 9 April 2007
}}</ref>

In 1983, he won the [[Helen B. Warner Prize for Astronomy]] given by the [[American Astronomical Society]] in recognition of "his many outstanding contributions to a wide range of dynamical problems in both solar-system and galactic dynamics".<ref name = HUBROUWER /><ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.aas.org/grants/awards.html|publisher = American Astronomical Society|title = AAS Prizes and Awards|accessdate = 9 April 2007|url-status = dead|archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20070404093144/http://www.aas.org/grants/awards.html|archivedate = 4 April 2007|df = dmy-all}}</ref>
